title: PPFAS Fund Chief Rajeev Thakkar Defends Strategy as Cash Drops to Lowest in Two Years
excerpt: India's largest actively managed equity fund has deployed its once-record cash pile into beaten-down IT stocks and private banks, with its CIO arguing that AI pessimism around the outsourcing sector is overblown.
body:
• PPFAS Mutual Fund's Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund, India's largest actively managed equity fund with $14.9 billion in assets, has reduced cash holdings from a peak of 25% to around 10% as equity valuations improve.
  • CIO Rajeev Thakkar has made a contrarian bet on Indian IT stocks, increasing the fund's technology allocation by 33% since January even as the Nifty IT Index posts its worst year since 2008.
  • The fund's top holdings remain concentrated in HDFC Bank, Power Grid, and ITC, with private banks accounting for nearly a quarter of the portfolio.
  • Thakkar has dismissed concerns that AI poses an existential threat to India's IT services industry, invoking Jevons' Paradox to argue that cheaper services will drive higher demand.

Rajeev Thakkar, the chief investment officer of PPFAS Mutual Fund, is pushing back against critics of his fund's recent underperformance by pointing to a rapidly improving opportunity set in Indian equities — and deploying the proof in real time by moving aggressively into sectors the rest of the market has abandoned.

Deploying the Cash Pile

The Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund, which manages approximately ₹1.41 lakh crore ($14.9 billion), had built up cash reserves to as high as 25% of assets by early 2026, a level that drew scrutiny from investors and industry peers. That number has dropped steadily — to 18.94% in March, 15.5% in April, and around 14% by May — as Thakkar found opportunities worth buying during a correction that sent the Nifty 50 to its weakest stretch in two years.

"The number is around 15% now. We are close to fully invested, so it's not that there is something unusual," Thakkar said at Groww's India Investor Festival in May. "But look at the past 24 months — headline indices like the Nifty 50 have not beaten commercial paper returns. So when we are in cash, we get commercial paper returns."

The fund's equity allocation has climbed to roughly 84% as of early August, up from 67% a year ago, according to fund data from Tickertape. The shift marks a decisive end to the defensive posture that had characterized PPFAS's approach through most of 2025.

"Wherever we are seeing reasonable valuations and reasonably good prospects, we are investing in those spaces. We are sticking with cash-flow generating businesses, and businesses which have value here and now."

— Rajeev Thakkar, CIO, PPFAS Mutual Fund

The Contrarian IT Bet

The most striking move has been in Indian IT services. While most flexi-cap funds have slashed IT exposure by roughly 27% since January, PPFAS has gone the other direction, increasing its technology allocation from 6.97% to 9.25% in four months — a 33% increase, according to ET Money.

The buying has concentrated in India's top-tier names. Exposure to Infosys rose 50%, TCS increased 41%, and HCL Technologies climbed 15% within the portfolio. The fund now has nearly 19% allocated to the technology sector overall, with IT Services and Consulting its second-largest sector holding behind private banks, Bloomberg reported.

The NSE Nifty IT Index is headed for its worst annual performance since 2008, down over 27% this year as investors fret that AI will erode demand for traditional outsourcing. Accenture's weak forecast in June only deepened the selloff. The index now trades at 15.7 times 2026 estimated earnings, down from 21.2 times a year ago.

Thakkar sees opportunity where others see an existential threat. "This whole pessimism that everything will be brought back in-house and no one will outsource any work, or these models will be so efficient that end-to-end everything will be done by the models and no humans will be required — I don't see that pessimism as being realistic," he told Bloomberg.

He has invoked Jevons' Paradox — the principle that when technology makes something cheaper, overall consumption tends to increase — to argue that AI-driven productivity gains in IT services could expand the addressable market rather than shrink it.

Portfolio Positioning

Beyond IT, PPFAS has been loading up on private-sector banks, which now account for nearly a quarter of the portfolio. HDFC Bank remains the fund's single largest holding at 8.33%, followed by Power Grid Corporation at 6.23%, ITC at 6.07%, ICICI Bank at 5.52%, and Coal India at 5.35%, according to August portfolio data.

During March's market crash, the fund bought HDFC Bank shares worth ₹1,866 crore, added ₹563 crore of ICICI Bank, and accumulated ₹861 crore of Kotak Mahindra Bank, Nuvama Institutional Equities data showed. On the sell side, Reliance Industries and Jio Financial Services were the largest exits.

Addressing Underperformance

The Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund returned approximately 1% over the past year, trailing many flexi-cap peers. Over a decade, however, it remains the category's second-best performer with annualized returns of nearly 17.8%, according to the Association of Mutual Funds in India.

For Indian mutual fund investors watching their SIPs underperform during a difficult stretch for domestic equities — foreign investors have withdrawn nearly $30 billion from Indian stocks this year — Thakkar's message is patience. "Equity investing should be for at least five years," he has said repeatedly. "Over that period, events like wars begin and end, but they don't materially impact long-term outcomes."

The question for PPFAS unitholders is whether the cash deployment into beaten-down IT stocks and banks will look prescient or premature. Thakkar is betting that valuations, after two years of time correction and recent price correction, have finally reached levels that justify conviction buying. The market will deliver its verdict in the quarters ahead.
nri_angle: PPFAS is one of the most popular mutual funds among NRI investors, and Thakkar's views on IT stocks directly affect the sector that employs millions across the Indian diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
